terms.grammar: verb phrase; intendō, third conjugation; with ad or in and the accusative, or the dative
evidence: Cic. Ac. 2.46 (Lewis & Short): parum dēfīgunt animōs et intendunt in ea quae perspicua sunt
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to direct one’s thoughts or attention to any thing”.

terms.grammar: adjective (participle of intendō); with the dative
verb phrase; dēfīgō, third conjugation; with in and the accusative

terms.gloss: throw oneself into, apply oneself to
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; with in or ad and the accusative, or the dative
evidence: Tac. Dial. 3 (Lewis & Short): tōtō pectore novae cōgitātiōnī
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to bend one’s attention to, to apply or devote one’s self to”.

evidence: Ter. Ph. 350: quīn tū hoc age
terms.comment: Lewis & Short s.v. agō: “to give attention to, to attend to, to mind, heed”; Hoc age! is “concentrate!”.

evidence: M-O s.v. focal point, focus (in optics)
terms.comment: Classically the hearth (see hearth); the sense of a focal point goes back to Kepler (1604), as Morgan–Owens notes.

phrases.latin: seu fossam fodiēns pālae innīxus seu cum arāret, operī certē, id quod cōnstat, agrestī intentus
phrases.english: Whether he was digging a ditch, leaning on his spade, or ploughing, he was certainly, as everyone agrees, intent on his farm work.

phrases.latin: ceu quondam tortō volitāns sub verbere turbō, quem puerī magnō in gȳrō vacua ātria circum intentī lūdō exercent
phrases.english: like a top spinning under the twisted whip, which boys, intent on their game, drive in a wide circle round the empty halls
